newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy to firm if reforms tackled - Mitsuzuka.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy to firm if reforms tackled - Mitsuzuka.

text.p: Japan's economy will likely become firmer after the April-June quarter of this year, if Japan tackles various reform issues with utmost effort, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a news conference on Tuesday.
"We must tackle these reforms with the utmost effort. In doing so, the economy will become firmer after the first quarter (of the 1997/98 fiscal year)," he said.
He added that, looking at current economic conditions, he was confident Japan would be able to achieve the government's growth target for this fiscal year.
The government has set a growth target of 1.9 percent for fiscal 1997/98.

Mitsuzuka also said he understands that there will be some deflationary effects from Japan's fiscal and economic reforms, but added, "There is no doubt that the base of the economy has become firmer."
In order to make its economic base more solid, Japan needs to tackle deregulation and administrative and economic reforms, he said.
He also said that currency rates seem to be stabilising as the Group of Seven (G7) nations have adhered to the agreement they reached in Washington in April.
The markets will also eventually judge correctly that Japanese banks are steadily dealing with their problem loans, he said.
Asked about the schedule for drawing up a fiscal reform bill, Mitsuzuka said that he hoped to have it ready as soon as possible.
"We hope to announce the outline of the bill by the end of this parliamentary session," he said. The current session of parliament ends later this month.

He added that the various ministries will draft their budget requests for fiscal year 1998/99 in line with numerical targets released earlier on Tuesday by a panel led by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Japanese ministries usually submit their budget requests to the Finance Ministry by the end of August.
